## Common cold

The common cold was a mundane infectious disease.

Acquisition
It was (falsely) believedIt's a common misconception that the common cold arises from cold weather or a chill. Nevertheless, this information is included for faithfulness to the source text and setting. that being chilly led to catching the common cold. For example, a risk of catching the common cold was one of many reasons that adventurers were warned not to sleep in metal armor or to travel during cold or rainy weather.

Effects
Sufferers of the common cold experienced fits of coughing and sneezing, which could disrupt the casting of spells or the conducting of rituals. Colds varied from mild to severe, although even severe infections were seen as merely annoying and uncomfortable compared to other, more fatal diseases.

Treatment
The common cold was easy to cure with magical healing however it was generally seen as too trivial to warrant the use of spells, thus some priests saw it as beneath the scope of their healing duties. However, the Temple of Gond in Tilverton was said to treat the common cold in the mid–14 century DR.

The common cold could also be treated effectively by mundane means. Remedies for the common cold were offered at apothecary shops (such as Mother's Cupboard in Raven's Bluff), where they sold for 1 gp as of the mid-to-late 14 century DR. Other remedies said to work for treating the common cold included myrrh and horsetail, as well as mallow, catnip, chives, garlic, ginger, mustard, and rose.

The halflings of Luiren had learned a special skill of medicinal cooking that involved making curative foods using Luiren spring cheese, and apprentice cooks knew how to prepare meals that could cure many normal diseases, including the common cold.

History
The small settlement of Kin Elbhaz in Maztica was famous as a place of such good fortune that the common cold was the worst disease with which they had to contend.

Notable Carriers
 Coll, a young thief who tried to flee Baldur's Gate in the, who caught a cold while hanging out around the docks without any shoes.

## Consecrated ground

Consecrated ground was a daily prayer available to clerics during the post-Spellplague era that temporarily consecrated an area with radiant energy.

Effects
Through prayer a cleric casting consecrated ground caused jagged and crackling lines of radiant light to spread across an area of ground of their choosing, moving in a web-like manner. Consecrated ground could be sustained by the caster and while active the area of effect could be moved to anywhere within  of the ground that was originally consecrated. Any enemy that stood within the area would be harmed by the radiant energy emanating from the ground, while any injured allies would be moderately healed.

History
In the, a party of four Daggerdalesmen adventurers were summoned to the mines of Tethyamar by the Banite priestess Lorin-Aria to kill the Zhent wizard Rezlus and put an end to his plans to conquer Daggerdale and the greater Dalelands region. Among this party of adventurers was a dwarf cleric who knew the prayer consecrated ground.

## Collar of animal control

Collars of animal control were enchanted animal collars that allowed one to force animals to obey mental commands.

Description
A collar of animal control was made of a thick leather, covered in markings and runes sacred to the deity Malar. Each collar bore a miniature iron chain.

Powers
These collars could be resized to fit around the neck of any animal. Once successfully put on an animal, the miniature chain on a collar of animal control would detach and those who held it would have control over the animal in a manner similar to the spell dominate animal. However, this mental link would end if the matching chain was not being held or if the animal was more than  away from the wielder. Additionally, if given a command that was obviously self-destructive, an animal might try to fight back against the command, potentially breaking the enchantment.

History
In the mid–14 century DR, Kazok a member of the Malarite organization Furious Hunt, terrorized the town of Berlingford in the Silver Marches with packs of wild dogs and wolves that he and his thugs commanded with collars of animal control. This domination of the local wolves angered the awakened wolf Felinal, whose master had been kidnapped by Kazok, but it was reluctant to attack the Malarites lest it fall victim to their collars of animal control.

## Corpse of despair

Corpses of despair were a variety of zombie that existed in the period between the Spellplague and the Second Sundering. They were created by necromancers from the corpses of those that had ended their own lives after being overcome with feelings of despair, loss, and hopelessness.

Description
A corpse of despair was physically distinguished from other zombies by their faces, which bore a frozen look of anguish that they had at the moment of their death. They also bore signs of the means by which they had taken their own life, such as a noose around the neck, signs of poisoning, or slit wrists.

Ability
Corpses of despair uniquely emanated a psychic aura of palpable, crushing despair and hopelessness around them that could afflict the minds of living creatures, dazing them, and potentially putting them in a lethal downward spiral unless they resisted the effect. Like other zombies they were resistant to harm from necrotic energy, but vulnerable to radiant energy.

Combat
Like most zombies, a corpse of despair was an unarmed combatant that fought to the point of destruction. They lashed out at whatever was closest to them, but focused their fists towards those dazed by their aura of gloom.

History
Around the late 15 century DR, a human necromancer from the Bleak Academy was operating in Tymanther, in an ancient Untheri burial site near Ruinspoke. Deep within a mausoleum at the burial site, the necromancer created a number of corpses of despair through use of the spell undead servitor.It is not specified in the adventure whether the ruins being explored belonged to Unther or Tymanchebar. However, due to the adventure only making note of ruins of "the old Untheric Empire" and the presence of a Lathanderite sarcophagus in the mausoleum, it stands to reason the ruins were from Unther.

## Cookbooks of the Underdark

Cookbooks of the Underdark was a set of four volumes of drow cookbooks that covered such diverse ingredients as mushrooms, fungus, molds, spores, and even meats, penned some years before 1371 DR.

Description
Each of these tomes was bound in a high quality expensive lizardhide.

Contents
The set consisted of four volumes, each collected at least ten recipes with detailed instructions and other relevant information that could be a valuable boon for any, even the most skilled cookery artisan. Volume I was simply titled Mushrooms. It included such recipes as mushroom paste, mushroom steak, spiced mushroom soup, sautéed mushrooms, fungus-breaded mushrooms, mushroom salad, spidermeat-stuffed mushrooms, boiled mushroom surprise, slivered k'li mushrooms, and, of corse, mushroom gravy. Volume II was titled Fungus and listed recipes for hot fungus cereal, dried fungus treat, scalloped gray fungus, fungus in wine sauce, pungent fungus rolls, spongy fungi dip, marinated fungus spread, fungus cake, fragrant fungi pie, and fungus fingers. Book III was alluringly named Molds and Spores. The recipes included were: fried mold muffins under glass, thick mold pudding, golden moldies, moldenberry sauce, glazed mold with spore icing, chocolate spores, mold and spore casserole, spore delights, fluffy spore cake, and the most appetizing of the bunch – moldy bread. Lastly, Volume IV – Meat Lovers, included such foods as steamed mice casserole, hot rat haunches, batwing salad & spore dressing, eyeless fish steaks, sauteed bat-rat turnovers, carrion crawler soup, glazed cave cricket tenders, minced kobold flanks, pureed slug over otyugh roast, and twice-basted stirge.

History
Cookbooks of the Underdark were recovered from the buried and abandoned Temple of Lolth near the trail that led to the town of Mossbridges in the Vast in the . The wizard named Tromor Zem hired a team of adventurers from the Living City to delve into the ruined temple's depths. The Cookbooks of the Underdark were discovered alongside Rourathek's spellbook in a spider-infested webbed room. The books were believed to had been taken to the city of Ravens Bluff by the hiring adventurers after the task was completed.

## Coal golem

Coal golems were humanoid shaped constructs constructed out of coal, as well as the elemental energies of earth and fire.

Description
The cinders of rare woods and coals that composed their powerful bodies were always hot and burning, with two particularly large glowing cinders acting as the eyes, and were all held in place by an open iron frame. Because their coals were always in a state of burning a coal golem constantly emitted steam, it regularly shed bits of sparks or ash, and a hissing sound was made whenever it attacked.

Coal golems sported stocky legs and their arms extended down to their knees. They moved with slow, clumsy gaits. On average they stood  tall and weighed about .

Behavior
Whenever a coal golem engaged in combat there was a miniscule chance that the elemental spirit trapped inside it would break free of its constraints and go berserk, attacking the nearest living creature or, if no creature was near, smashing or setting alight nearby objects that were smaller than it. If nearby the golem's creator could attempt to regain control by speaking firmly and persuasively to it. Some sages speculated that this behavior was due to the conflicting mix of elemental earth and fire.

Attacking a coal golem was cold-based magic was liable to enrage them, regardless of whether they inflicted any harm or not, and draw their attention towards the caster.

Abilities
Like all golems, a coal golem had innate immunity to most spells, spell-like abilities, or other supernatural effects. Spells like cone of cold and ice storm could slow their movements, while Otiluke's freezing sphere could outright freeze them in place temporarily. Fire-based magical effects could break a coal golem free of these impediments and repair their body of damage.

Combat
A coal golem was typically armed with an oversized metal longspear that glowed red from the heat of the golem's body. A regular tactic of theirs was to ignite flammable objects in their surroundings, thereby making the area of combat more dangerous for their opponent.

Ecology
Languages
Like most golems these constructs could not speak, but unlike other golems they could not understand Common. Instead a coal golem could only understand commands given in Ignan.
Relationships
Coal golems were most commonly created by creature with an affinity for fire and that thrived in intensely hot environments, such as fire giants mastered in arcane magic and salamanders. The latter were most commonly known to create them and even believed by some to be the first to do so. Salamanders regularly used them to guard their forges or for mere slave labor, while fire giants sometimes created them solely to act as decorative mobile statues for their fortresses.

## Council Army

The Council Army was the official state army of Amn, handled by the Dahaunarch of the Council of Six and later the Council of Five. It was a professional military organization that protected the realm and its interests. It was accompanied by the Council Navy, which performed similar duties on the high seas.

Activities

The Council Army maintained and garrisoned the fortresses around Amn, as well as patrolled the roads, collected taxes, caught smugglers, and fought raiders. As an extension of the Council, the Army was fundamentally responsible for facilitating trade by ensuring that roads and markets were kept open, with all that entailed.

The Council Navy acted likewise on the Great Sea. It was a small navy of fast, light ships based in Murann that was primarily concerned with chasing away Nelanther Isles pirates and escorting merchants, not fighting fleet battles. It was expected that merchants would organize themselves in convoys and hire private warships as needed, and the Navy was intended to supplement this security in the event that pirates massed into their own fleets. In the case of dire emergency, the Navy reserved the right to force private vessels to join them in battle, though it was never used. The fortunes of the Council Navy tended to rise and fall along with that of the navies of Tethyr and Calimshan, as the strength and activities of each navy affected the prosperity and boldness of pirates in the region.

Organization
The competence of the officer class was extremely variable, as they were often promoted based on the influence of their families rather than their ability. As a result, some postings were commanded by corrupt schemers or incapable buffoons, while others were dutiful and thoughtful leaders. The morale and quality of the rank-and-file ranged widely because of this, with some commanders fostering mutinous or incapable troops, while the best inspired loyalty and excellence in their company. A particular fear of the Council was that the common soldiers could have stronger loyalties towards a popular commander over the Council, and thus be willing to take part in rebellion against them.

Outside of the officer ranks, veteran soldiers were called Legionaries, while the most elite of the Council Army were called Centurions.

The Army had a desertion problem around the distant and unpopular posting at Hillfort Keshla. Deserting troops would hide in the hills and functionally become bandits, preying opportunistically on travelers while avoiding large fights. They sometimes joined with hobgoblins to form larger bands.

As befitting soldiers, the worship of Tempus was most popular among Army members, with Tyr, Torm, Ilmater, and Helm having smaller congregations. The Golden Fortress contained chapels and shrines to many gods in order to serve the spiritual needs of the inhabitants.

Equipment
Common soldiers were equipped with basic but functional gear such as brigandine and chainmail armor, shortswords, spears, longswords, longbows, and crossbows. Officers and veterans were usually found with full plate or plate mail, and often brought their own powerful magical items to supplement their kit, especially if they came from a wealthy family. Morion helmets were extremely common equipment, as were more decorative "winged" helmets.

Base of Operations
 Athkatla held a garrison 4,000 soldiers, and the core of the Council Navy made up of eight warships and 900 marines.
 The Golden Fortress of Eshpurta was the Army's headquarters in eastern Amn, and served as an academy for training new recruits. It normally held about 25,000 soldiers, officers, trainers, and support staff.
 Citadel Rashturl and Citadel Amnur guarded the northern border of Amn and normally had garrisons of 720 officers and soldiers.
 Hillforts Keshla, Ishla, and Torbold guarded Amn's southern border along the South Road through the Tejarn Hills, each having a garrison of about 315 soldiers and officers. Keshla in particular was used as a dumping ground for failed soldiers and political liabilities.
 Keczulla had a garrison southeast of the city made up of 800 infantry and 200 cavalry that patrolled the length of the Gem Road and along the Eshpurta Road between Amnwater and Axe Bridge.
 Murann hosted a small navy from the Council for militia use, as well as a Council Navy detachment made up of fast cutters and caravels.
 Nashkel had a strong garrison that guarded the town and nearby strategically important iron mine.

Relationships

Despite being the state army of Amn, the Council Army worked with (and against) numerous other militant organizations in both regular everyday activities and during wartime emergencies. The Army made up about half of the total military forces directly controlled by the Council itself, with the rest made up of the Councillor's various personal retinues of soldiers, mercenaries, and agents.

 Each city had a heavily-armed militia loyal to the local mayor or council that handled internal policing, justice, and regional patrols, often overlapping duties with the Council Army. These included the Shield Militia of Eshpurta, the Bargemen of Crimmor and Crimmor Guard, the Gem Guard of Keczulla, the Ring Knights of Riatavin, and the Harbor Guard of Murann.
 Magical support and the policing of wizards was provided by the first secretly, then openly Council-controlled Cowled Wizards.
 Spycraft and assassinations were handled by the Shadow Thieves, who were secretly controlled by the Council.
 Major temples in Amn could raise their own small armies if necessary, either from gold-hired mercenaries or their own faithful formed into crusades.
 Families and mercantile companies were allowed to raise their own private militias of up to 500 soldiers, and companies could also collect taxes on behalf of the Council.
 Mercenaries were hired on small and large scales by the Council for certain situations, such as the Golden Legion being hired to explore the western ocean, and later becoming the official armed forces of New Amn.
 Adventurer companies were not permitted to roam freely and cause mischief, but were required to register and pay for licenses. They were also used as agents of the Council as needed.

History

In 1356 DR, the Council Army took part in the First Dragonspear War, fighting the devils and their allies in the Greenfields.

The rebellion of Riatavin in the  caused the Army to muster in preparation for a full-scale assault on the city, fighting the forces of Tethyr if necessary. This prospective military campaign was interrupted at the last moment by the Sothillisian War breaking out, and the Army quickly redeployed in order to fight against the well-led goblins, giants, ogres and kobolds that threatened Esmeltaran, Imnescar, Trademeet, and Murann. Murann was blockaded by a fleet of pirates led by the Black Alaric, overwhelming the Council Navy at hand.

The war turned into a nightmare for the Army, as troops for the region had been withheld based on the suspicion that Major Tharundar Olehm would lead a rebellion, Captain Amlos Xornnag deserted and gave aid to the enemy, and the Council itself was unwilling to prosecute the war too aggressively for fear of spending too much money. This resulted in the Army vacillating between a complete lack of orders that left them passive and vulnerable, and overbold attacks that cost grievous casualties without meaningful gain. Many commanders were paralyzed and frustrated by the confused situation, and some officers committed near-mutiny by forcing their commanders to commit to the war instead of pausing indefinitely. Despite their best efforts, the Army only managed to retake Trademeet after it was razed, and was forced to unenthusiastically besiege Esmeltaran from a camp in the Scimitar.

As the Council of Six dithered over how much money to invest in the military campaign, the armies in the field stalemated. The main breakthrough of the war actually came from the Selûnite church in 1372 DR, when it raised an army of crusaders with the aim of recapturing Murann. Striking forth in the spring, the crusaders retook Imnescar, and in autumn the forces of Sothillis were briefly redirected in a march against Tethyr in the Bloody Fall.

The following year the Selûnite crusade managed to recapture the pass through the Small Teeth to Trademeet and cut off the supply lines to Esmeltaran, and allowed the Council Army to finally retake it in the autumn. The Selûnites were joined by Cyricists of the Dark Embrace and Loviatans from the Black Spires of the Maiden, forming the unlikely alliance of the Army of Three Stars as they fought together.

The Sothillisian War was interrupted in the  by the Stinger War, and the Trade Way Truce was called as both sides dealt with the unexpected tlincalli invasion. Over the next century, Murann remained in the hands of Sothillis and grew the realm of Muranndin around itself, becoming a persistent stronghold of pirates, bandits and monsters that threatened Amn. This became a long period of exhausting skirmishes in the region for the Army, only resolved well after 1479 DR when Muranndin was finally destroyed.

Members
In the 14 century DR, the Council Army had the following soldiers and officers:

 General Labak Craumerdaun of the Golden Fortress.
 Colonel Gladdos Wintosnip of the Keczulla garrison.
 Major Tharundar Olehm of Hillfort Torbold.
 Commander Balacer Macefist of the Golden Fortress.
 Commander Endrick Hardlm of Citadel Amnur.
 Commander Reyni Delapond of Citadel Rashturl.
 Captain Amlos Xornnag of Hillfort Ishla.
 Captain Arbas Rosznar of Hillfort Keshla.
 Captain Arilan Krimmevol of Citadel Amnur.
 Captain Belars Orhotek of the Athkatla garrison.
 Captain Brage of the Nashkel garrison.
 Lieutenant Dannal Harftevor of the Cavalry.
 Squad Leader Namble Swiftleg of Army Squad 4, Second Battalion of the Amnwater Blues Regiment.
 Logan Coprith, a soldier in Citadel Rashturl.
 Bardolan, a soldier in Nashkel.
 Korienna Redarm, an officer who deserted.

## Cortryn

Cortryn was a militaristic duchy of the post-Shoon Imperium period that sought to attain imperial glory between the 5–8 centuries DR.

Geography
Cortryn controlled a wide area of land east of Lake Esmel, ranging from the Troll Mountains in the north to the Tejarn Hills in the south. Eshpurta was its northernmost city.

History
The northern frontier of Calimshan was long known as the Ralamnish Ridings, as part of the greater Calishar Emirates. As the Emirate of Amin developed on the western coast, the interior region was left mostly unsettled. The kingdom of Valashar was founded in 361 DR by Lord Ashar Tornamn of Tethyr, who attempted an ambitious campaign of conquest and colonization. This  resulted in the disastrous war with Cormyr in 376 DR, his own execution, and the abandonment of the realm.

Following the dissolution of the Shoon Imperium in 450 DR, Cortryn was founded on the former lands of Valashar in the, resettled by people from Tethyr and Calimshan led by the noble Kadar el Aktorral. Kadar claimed an obscure imperial title that gave him the right to the land, and marched with an army of hired mercenaries. The new duchy took control of a wide swathe of land stretching from the Troll Mountains to the Tejarn Hills, including the brutal conquest of the halfling realm of Meiritin.

The expansionist realm came into conflict with Amn in 520 DR, and King Imnel Torlath I died in battle with the forces of Cortryn.

After decades of abuse and enslavement by the domineering rulership of Cortryn, Bellabar Huntinghorn of Meiritin led an exodus of halflings away in the . They traveled far to the north and settled around Secomber with their kin, then joined with the realm of Phalorm. The remaining halflings of Meiritin mostly abandoned the province in 523 DR, leaving it empty.

At some point, the ruling lord Bevedaur went on a serpent hunt in the swamps at the mouth of the Winding Water, the future site of Lathtarl's Lantern. His party was attacked by an army of lizardfolk and the whole company wiped out.

Cortryn was overtaken in 731 DR by the Ring of Eyes, a cabal of five beholders and their minions. The ruling family of Cortryn was destroyed and lands conquered, and the beholders waged an ongoing war against the elves of Shilmista and King Strohm III of Tethyr. This lasted until the  when the mage Tashara of the Seven Skulls slew the beholders and shattered their domain.

The former realm was finally absorbed by Amn in the, with Eshpurta going on to become Amn's eastern capital and major military base.

A conspiracy to recreate Cortryn emerged in 1370 DR, organized by the Knights of the Shield. They sought to restore the old monarchy of Amn via the installation of Pehllus Tanislove, and return Meiritin and Cortryn as independent realms once more. Under this scheme, the rebellious city of Riatavin would become the seat of the duchy with Mundal Krimmevol as leader.

## Colossus of Dukar

The Colossus of Dukar was a gigantic monument in the underwater city of Myth Nantar depicting the near-mythical triton of the same name, the first Grand Master of the Dukars, an ancient Serôsian order of wizards.

Location
The Colossus stood within the Dukar Quarter of Myth Nantar, next to the Dukars' Academy, with its legs straddling the entrance to Dukar's tomb.

Description
This statue stood  tall, making it the tallest structure in the city. It was completely carved from lucent coral, which naturally gave off a bright glow and thus made the Colossus the source of one-fourth of all light in Myth Nantar. It depicted Dukar with his legendary Grandmaster's Tapal raised overhead in his right arm.

The Colossus was notably the site of one of the few portals within the city that the dukar Qos would freely divulge to anyone. This hidden portal opened to the former gates of the city of Akhanmyr and in order to activate it one had to swim in a loop around the Colossus's head three times before swimming straight upwards.

History
In, a group of dukar of the Jhimari and Numos orders went rogue, wanting to transform Myth Nantar into their own city-state by the name of Nantarum. Sometime later around, on the day the merfolk king Ristan laid siege against them, the thirty rogue dukars were standing around the Colossus of Dukar as the city's mythal let off bursts of magical energy. The dukars were later found by the attackers to have been petrified into coral statues, lining the avenue leading to the Dukars' Academy, their faces frozen with looks of contrition.

On Marpenoth 30, 1369 DR, when Iakhovas and his forces launched an assault upon the city of Myth Nantar the Oghmanyte bard Pacys stood atop the Colossus of Dukar, overlooking the battle. From there he played upon his instrument saceddar, singing a ballad he had written for Myth Nantar's defenders to magically inspire them.

Late in the year 1370 DR, among the thirty petrified dukars a sea elf of the Order of Jhimar by the name of Radom mysteriously returned to life, leaving only twenty-nine petrified dukars around the Colossus.

## Constabulary Branch One

Constabulary Branch One was the first of the three major watch headquarters of the Eileanar enclave of Netheril, alongside Branch Two and Branch Three.

Location
The building was found on the northern rim of the enclave, handling the crimes in that region.

Structure
The ground floor of the building was partially publicly accessible, with three receptionists who handled and guided visitors. A large room behind the reception area held the desks, comfy chairs, filing cabinets, and crystal balls of twenty low-ranking constables who worked there when they weren't out patrolling the streets.

The cellar level was made up of an expansive maze of 200 jail cells, with the entire level impossible to magically enter or exit, and causing incredibly dangerous backlash effects against teleportation magic.

The upper level of the structure was home to the offices of the highest-ranking constables and commissioners who reported directly to Karsus and his trusted followers such as Andoris Derathar. The Chief of Constables Zacharia was assisted by the loyal and dutiful Underchiefs Chanteclaire, Chantonay, and Flamininus. Chantonay was responsible for protecting the building via magical and quasimagical items, spells, and other magical effects, while Flamininus performed divinations and similar augury magics, using them to locate criminals and verify personal accounts during interviews and court proceedings.

Defenses
The jail level of the building was extremely heavily warded against intrusion, thanks to one of Chatonay's friends weaving a complex web of magical defenses. Magical infiltration was impossible, and teleportation was potentially subject to extreme backlash:

 Spell failure: The spell failed and had no effect, sparing the caster from a worse fate.
 Duo dimension: The caster was subject to duo-dimension, else be briefly stunned and ricocheted.
 Echo: As the caster bounced off of the wards, a clone was generated that was typically sane though with a limited lifespan of several months. If the clone managed to kill the original it would become permanent, otherwise it dissipated once the magic ran out.
 Reflection: The caster was teleported up to  away from the jails in a random direction.
 Refraction: An extreme effect befell the interloper. This included a crippling magical injury, a forced reincarnation, a reversal of alignment, a sex change, a permanent weakening of ability, or a permanent boosting of ability while all their magical gear was sucked into the Negative Energy plane.
 Ricochet: The caster was transported to a new location according to the spell used. Intra-planar teleportation sent them to a random spot on Toril, while spells such as plane shift sent them to a random plane entirely.

## Constabulary Branch Two

Constabulary Branch Two was the second of the three major watch headquarters of the Eileanar enclave of Netheril, alongside Branch One and Branch Three.

Location
The building was towards the western side of the enclave, close to the Academy of Mentalist Study.

Structure
The ground floor of the building was partially publicly accessible, with three receptionists who handled and guided visitors. A large room behind the reception area held the desks, comfy chairs, filing cabinets, and crystal balls of twenty low-ranking constables who worked there when they weren't out patrolling the streets.

The cellar level was made up of an expansive maze of 200 jail cells, heavily patrolled by constables on guard duty.

The upper level of the structure was home to the offices of the highest-ranking constables and commissioners who reported directly to Karsus and his trusted followers such as Andoris Derathar. The unscrupulous Chief of Constables Michallon was assisted by the opportunistic Underchiefs Bengel, Bias, Ezeddeen, and Hacklander, each in charge of 12 constables.

Activities
The Chief Constable kept a wide web of criminal contacts that he coordinated with, earning large amounts of money as his lawful forces exterminated the competition. The Underchiefs were his co-conspirators in this, and continued to obey his directions out of a combination of fear and greed. They cultivated a sense of awe and grandeur in the lower constables, who all believed that their commanders were the most upstanding and virtuous figures in the enclave, with Michallon the most heroic of all.

Defenses
The jails lacked the magical wardings of Branch One, instead relying solely on its guard patrols.

## Constabulary Branch Three

Constabulary Branch Three was the third of the three major watch headquarters of the Eileanar enclave of Netheril, alongside Branch One and Branch Two.

Location
The building was on the eastern edge of the enclave, near Dundaden's Armory.

Structure

The ground floor of the building was partially publicly accessible, with three receptionists who handled and guided visitors. A large room behind the reception area held the desks, comfy chairs, filing cabinets, and crystal balls of twenty low-ranking constables who worked there when they weren't out patrolling the streets.

The upper level of the structure was home to the offices of the highest-ranking constables and commissioners who reported directly to Karsus and his trusted followers such as Andoris Derathar.

The cellar level was an extensive underground complex made up of 200 jail cells.

Activities
The dutiful Chief of Constables Emblemat was assisted by his loyal Underchiefs Cadogen, Goddard, and Morian. The branch's constables were proud and hard-working, but they struggled with the constant low-level, petty crime that seemed endemic to eastern Karsus, and as a result they were overworked, short on sleep, and at times felt hopeless in the face of their task.

Emblemat was not passive in the face of these challenges, and used several methods to shore up the confidence and enthusiasm of his constables. One policy used nowhere else in Netheril allowed the constables to keep the reward money for every criminal they caught, which greatly improved their attitudes.

## Cordial

Cordials were a type of strong liquor of some medicinal properties.

Availability
On the Sword Coast North, medicines, wines, and cordials were produced by the monks of Goldenfields in the Dessarin Valley. Bhephel's Bottles in the North Ward of Waterdeep dealt in exotic wines and cordials. In the city of Baldur's Gate, The Blade and Stars inn served a sweet and thick cordial – a mixture of cherries liquified in dessert red wine. In Sundabar, firestar wine from The Firestar Chariot, was a concoction of amber sherry and ruby cordial.

Cordials and brandies were available from Toss Your Tankard in Harrowdale and from I Shot an Arrow in Arrowmark of the Dalelands.

In the kingdom of Cormyr, namely in Arabel, Marsember, and Suzail, producers of medicinal cordials and physics were taxed same as producers of other alcoholic beverages, or "strong drinks." One such producer was the House of Morning in the town of Eveningstar that fermented, distilled, and bottled their own herbal cordials and physics that were sold to traveling merchants.

People of Sembia preferred to consume their coffee mixed with melted chocolate and flavored with cordials or liquors.

The Purple Lady of Westgate and its Lady of the House Ambra Indreth were known to serve teas and cordials to their guests.

In the city of Ravens Bluff, medicinal fiery cordials were sold by Rare and Fine Seashell Remedies of the Seaglimpse Neighborhood. The Sword Tables Dining Lounge, Rose's Tea Room, The Black Lotus, and the Fruits & More establishments in Ravens Bluff also offered a variety of cordials. The so-called Essence of Dryad drink claimed to be made using a pulp of a tree and a dryad who inhabited it, but in reality was a dryad-made cordial. And as of the late 14 century DR, the drink known as the Moonmint Cordial created by Rapheira Skyhawk was gaining popularity in the Living City.

In West Faerûn, cordials were popular in the nation of Tethyr. The Yardarm in Velen had a wide variety of cordial on offer, as well at the Stag Triumphant in Mosstone.

Ruby-red brissberry cordials were a popular libation in the land of Halruaa in the Shining South and in the town of Ashtarahh.

Drow of the Underdark distilled strong cordials from various fermented subterranean mushrooms. Some drow cordials were exported out of the drow lands to the surface nations. Similarly, elves of the ancient city of Myth Drannor consumed dawnberry cordials.

## Company of the Sundered Orc

The Company of the Sundered Orc was the name of one or two adventuring companies active on the Sword Coast in the mid-to-late 14 century DR.The Company of the Sundered Orc was mentioned twice, in "The Reports from Undermountain" and Return to Undermountain, both times as adventuring companies that explored Undermountain and were not seen again, but with contradictory times, places, and fates. Return (dated 1373 DR) puts it "over ten years ago", i.e., before 1363 DR, but "Reports" is set in 1368 DR. The former is on first level, the latter on the second. Return suggests they may have died and risen as ghosts, but "Reports" has been them captured by drow. While this might be the same company, "Reports" says they are "relatively new", which may not suit a group of five years' experience. It is possible these are two separate companies with coincidentally the same name, that the second company was reformed from surviving members of the first company, or that the Return event should be more recent than 1368 DR. Regardless, this article covers both adventuring companies.

Organization
The company had five members circa 1368 DR:
 Lorar the Slayer, a human fighter;
 Pelops, a.k.a. Shadowstriker, a halfling thief;
 Jared Rheloph, "the Pious", a human cleric of Ilmater;
 Cassandra Rulmac, a half-elf fighter and wizard; and
 Wynara Rulmac, a human wizard.

History
First Company
In the early 1360s DR, the Company of the Sundered Orc had started exploring the dungeons of Undermountain. On their first expedition, they discovered the Librarium on the first level, called the Dungeon Level, and returned alive to boast about its wonders. They kept its precise location to themselves, however, and arranged for several porters to join them on their next expedition to carry out its vast and eclectic collection of books and scrolls. They were not seen again as of 1373 DR and had presumably died there.

Second Company
The five adventurers—Lorar, Pelops, Jared, Cassandra, and Wynara—came together in Daggerford relatively recently as of 1368 DR and soon headed for Waterdeep, not yet even having a name for their company. En route, they encountered a small orc raiding band and destroyed them, so they named themselves for this event.

In Waterdeep, they went to the Yawning Portal inn and began exploring the dungeons of Undermountain as adventurers do. In the, they elected to locate a supposed treasure hoard on the second level, the Arcane Chambers, which the Waterdhavian merchant-adventurer Essimuth Lanys claimed to have sighted. They ventured down the well just after sunset on Eleint 2, and had not yet returned by the end of the month. The Tymoran priest Adama Miiralin stationed at the inn recorded this in his monthly report to High Priestess Seenroas Halvinhar.

In fact, all five of them had been captured by drow slavers in the Arcane Chambers and were soon to be transported to Skullport.

## Confidant of a Duke

Confidant of a Duke was a book penned by Golbraith Stredivas, friend and confidant of Duke Abdel Adrian, published sometime in or before the late 15 century DR.

Content
The recorded information in the Confidant of a Duke was a somewhat rambling account of a friendship between Abdel Adrian and Golbraith Stredivas. The two met after the Bhaalspawn became a Duke of Baldur's Gate and took on a habit of wandering the streets of the city incognito, wearing a hooded cloak. Abdel called it "taking the pulse of the town," and, as Golbraith supposed, this habit came from the Duke's humble upbringing among the scholars of Candlekeep.

During one such venture into the Lower City, Abdel met Golbraith at one of the terrace tables of the Elfsong Tavern. The two accidentally bought each other's drinks by calling the same waiter to them. The strangers stroke up a conversation, and when the Duke found out that Golbraith was an adventurer and a monster hunter, he showered the man with questions. On the next meeting, the Bhaalspawn revealed that he too was an adventurer once, and afterward, they met regularly at the Elfsong, turning conversations into a friendship. Many tendays later Golbraith realized that his new friend was the Grand Duke.

Finally, Confidant of a Duke continued on recording numerous meandering stories the men shared while sharing numerous tankards of ale.

History
In the, Confidant of a Duke could be found in the home of Golbraith Stredivas in the Gate's Lower City.

## Council of the Dragon

The Council of the Dragon was a noble moot called by King Foril Obarskyr I of Cormyr to discuss the ruling of the Realm.

Location
The Council of the Dragon was held in the Hall of Justice in Castle Obarksyr.

Activities
There was to be open discussion, and a vow of magically enforced loyalty to Prince Irvel Obarskyr, starting at highsun.

Outcome
In the eve of the council, blueflame ghosts murdered Seszgar Huntcrown, and then likely Gariskar Dauntinghorn and Draskos Crownsilver, raising alarm among the nobles. Then on the day of the council, following the machinations of the vampire archmage Manshoon, the room was flooded with deadly poison gas, demanding a day's delay.

When the moot was finally held, before any vows occurred, the nobles made a number of demands that while individually reasonable, would have not just nulled the Suzail Writ, but granted the nobility much more power than before. Several demands that ensued, such as that of Landrar Dathcloake, who demanded that nobles be able to form a council to control all of Cormyr, rather than the royal family, went even beyond. Obraerl Foulweather and Mulcaster Emmarask both pushed forward for this, despite Foril's position being that it was a red line for him. When the last one claimed this was the will of Alusair Obarskyr, her ghost manifested and denounced his position as a load of bull. Rather than back off, he doubled down, and claimed she wasn't really the princess; Alusair immediately walked through him, and he fell to the ground, twitching.

Things degenerated quickly after that, with many nobles forming a ring around the king, and a battle ensuing, in which at least one Highknight and one War Wizard died. After Prince Irvel Obarskyr's ironguard was tested, he was ushered out of the room just in time for a blueflame ghost to appear and start cutting down nobles. She disappeared after killing Lord Foulweather.

Then Amarune Whitewave, a mask dancer housing the consciousness of the fugitive wizard Elminster Aumar at the time, used a perfected version of the call bones spell to fatally debone every noble who attacked the King.

Aftermath
Predictably, word on the streets was that Cormyr had been plunged into civil war afterwards. There were a number of killings that could be assumed to have been precipitated by the opportunity, such as the death of Lord Windstag, for which no other cause was known. The rumors blew the situation out of proportion somewhat, claiming that the Royal Family had died, for instance.

## Corpse Market

The Corpse Market was the primary marketplace in the city of Evernight in the Shadowfell. It specialized in the sale of all manner of bodies, whether alive, dead, or undead.

Description
The Market stretched for multiple city blocks in every direction, and was packed with shops, stalls, and street vendors separated by tattered canvas shrouds. The market was drab and colorless, but illuminated by torchlight. It was a cacophony of merchants hawking their wares and shouting to drown out their competitors, thus making it the noisiest and liveliest part of Evernight. These merchants were predominantly undead beings selling bodies and body parts for consumption by other undead, but they also carried supplies—ranging from mundane tools to everything a necromancer might need—and zombie servants for rent. Customers milled about—mostly ghouls, skeletons, and vampires with the very occasional living person—making transactions with gold as in any other marketplace, although some merchants expected services or flesh as payment instead. Any living merchant wishing to do business and not end up as food had to acquire a special token that served as proof that they were to be left alone (although the tokens were not always necessary as most of the undead assumed that no living person would be foolish enough to visit the Market without such protection).

One corner of the Corpse Market was dominated by a large auction block made of bone and old wood, which was where living humanoids were sold (either as food or as slaves). Vendors had to attract their own crowds and customers if they wished to auction off their captives. Any efforts to disrupt these auctions attracted a hostile reprisal from the entire Market.

Location
The Corpse Market filled a walled area in the southern part of Evernight, and abutted the Graveyard to the west. It overlapped the same location as did the Main Graveyard of Neverdeath in Neverwinter on the Material Plane. It was well-known within Evernight that the boundary between the Shadowfell and the Material Plane was full of cracks at the Corpse Market, potentially allowing the undead to reach out and snatch unsuspecting victims from Neverwinter.

Near the Market was a fenced-off area where the merchants' workshops and storehouses were located. Any unauthorized visitor to this area was immediately assumed to be a spy or a thief, and was dealt with violently.

Services
Food
The Corpse Market specialized in meals for undead creatures who were too lazy or too busy to otherwise catch their food. This included not only living captives but meat and body parts for the city's ghouls as well as blood for the vampires. Ghoulish delicacies included pickled fingers and organs wrapped to go. Blood was kept fresh in jars or enchanted decanters of glass or ceramic, and higher-end merchants offered many types of blood from which to choose (e.g., from victims of any given species, age, sex, social status, or magical aptitude). One such blood shop was Sangora Sanguinaries.

Grafts
The Market sold animated body parts for the purpose of being attached to living creatures. These undead grafts ranged from limbs (such as for granting enhanced strength) to organs (such as for granting the limited uncanny abilities of creatures such as liches, mummys, or vampires). For an extra fee, a few merchants would also perform the complex and profane rites to graft these body parts onto their customers. The most famous of these merchants was a mad vampire surgeon named Sanjos Irridan.

Supplies
A wide range of mundane equipment, raw materials, tools, and weapons could be found at the Market, most of which were retrieved from the bodies of slain humanoids. In general, these supplies included the things that anymore—namely even the undead—might require, but the Market also sold oddities and luxuries, such as dead flowers, decorative canopic jars, decaying burial finery, and jewelry (often displayed on severed hands).

For necromancers, the Corpse Market carried everything from rare specimens of blood and bone for experimentation to profane holy symbols and fresh grave dust for rituals.

Undead for Hire
Zombie laborers and porters could be rented for 10 gp per day, plus a deposit that took the form of a chunk of flesh that was surgically removed from the buyer, alchemically treated to keep it preserved, and then reattached upon safe return of the rented zombies.

Sentient undead would occasionally rent or hire themselves out as guides, sometimes for coin and sometimes for their own amusement. Visitors to Evernight might hire such a guide to show them around or answer questions about the city (although honesty was not guaranteed). Information could cost 20 gp per question, or perhaps would only be provided in exchange for an answer to the guide's own questions. Sangora of Sangora Sanguinaries was known to offer directions and knowledge for such prices. Hiring a guide for a trip outside the city required a fee of at least 100 gp per day, although this increased for longer or more dangerous journeys and did not entail the guide's assistance in combat (nor their loyalty more generally). Certain special undead guides had the uncanny ability to smell different kinds of death or undead, and could be hired for a minimum of 200 gp per day to help an employer find the remains of a specific person, place, or creature.

History
As of the late 15 century DR, the Corpse Market was as bustling as any marketplace on Toril. Its most famous patron was a mysterious living man known as the Resurrectionist, who would spend hours each day examining the bodies and body parts as he searched for the remains of a certain long-dead person.

## Communion of Laughter

The Communion of Laughter was a worship service held by the church of Garl Glittergold on the 13 day of each month, a date considered auspicious in gnome folklore. It was a day-long celebration in which gnomes revered Garl Glittergold through a series of joyous activities.

Activities
Typically, the gnomes engaged in a period of quiet prayer and contemplation, danced on the temple's central dais, enjoyed a communal meal in which they shared food, told stories alongside displays of magic, and competed to tell jokes. This last event usually went until late in the night. Otherwise, the specific order of events varied with each temple.

Each attendee was encouraged to donate a piece of gold or a handful of gold dust, or other precious metal, as a tribute to Garl. The temple uses these donations to benefit the community as a whole.

Desperate to save the city from a war, she could've passed The Legend of Ansur to the adventurers, also known as the Absolute Adversaries, if she trusted them to defend the city and a confrontation with Wyll Ravengard had not turned bloody. Cordula Eltan believed that the legend of Ansur was true and the dragon could rise one time and only once time if called to defend the city of Baldur's Gate.

History

In the middle of the Sschindylryn invasion of Eveningstar, Cormul Haythorne joined his friends Ana Brabener and Torin Betrich in the search for the "Thread of the Weave", the mysterious war goal of the drow war. Torin insisted on taking action to save the village, and so the trio went into the King's Forest, presuming that the old abandoned Temple of Mystra would have something to do with what the drow wanted.

While Torin stayed to search the area, Cormul returned to Eveningstar and sought help from the overwhelmed Purple Dragons Constal Adamor Thellik, who delegated the rescue mission to a group of Eberronian heroes who were passing by. He was quite delighted when Ana was returned intact in the end.

## Corpse host

Corpse host was an arcane spell of the necromancy school that allowed a necromancer to temporarily transfer the consciousness or "life force" of a living creature into the corpse of a demihuman, human, or humanoid, thereby animating said corpse. Necromancers who chose not to recognize the schools of magic could obtain it through path magic.Path magic is an alternative system of rules for the spell progression and learning of spells by wizards for 2 edition Dungeons & Dragons. They could therefore be considered potentially non-canon.

Effects
This spell could only be cast upon a living target. A necromancer could not target an undead creature to be the host of a cadaver.

Whilst corpse host was active, the targeted living creature had a full range of capability for animating the corpse they inhabited. This included movement, performing actions, carrying things, and even casting spells. They could not, however, perform exacting tasks and handicrafts, such as lockpicking or sewing for example.

A cadaver affected by corpse host ceased to decay. Unless illusion magic was cast upon the corpse, it would appear to all eyes as being an undead creature. Any magical items it adorned would not pass their effects on to the recipient's living body. The cadaver could move a minimum distance of  from the living body, with this range extending further based upon the spellcaster's skills in magic. The active of the spell was a minimum of 1 day, likewise extending further based upon the individual necromancer's skills in magic.

If the cadaver moved outside of this effective range or into another plane, the mind of the recipient of corpse host would return to their living body and the cadaver would immediately collapse, resuming its original decay. Additionally, the recipient could at will leave the cadaver their were piloting and return to their original body. In both cases, there existed no chance of the recipient suffering any sort of shock to their system.

The targeted individual's mind was active simultaneously in both their original body and the corpse's, allowing them to hear, see, sense from both. They could also talk through the corpse, though their voice would come out in a hoarse variation of the corpse's original voice. The mind inhabiting the cadaver was subject to magical and psionic powers that affected the mind. For this same reason, the cadaver's senses could be fooled by illusions. Because the piloted corpse was not truly undead, it was unaffected by the clerical power turn undead, nor any spells or magics whose effects targeted the undead.

For the duration of corpse host, the targeted individual could not move their body – for this reason, people were often left to stand guard over the host body. The target could only make their original body blink, breath, and move its eyes. During this period the living creature's body was also not subject to the basic bodily needs of eating, drinking, and sleeping. Any physical attacks inflicted upon the cadaver would not transfer harm to the recipient's real body, though upon destruction of the cadaver or severance of the link between it and the target's real body, the recipient of corpse host experienced a shock to their system that carried a small chance of fatality.

Arcane spells that could sever the spiritual link between the cadaver and the living body included dispel magic, limited wish, and wish. Divine magic spells that could do the same included dispel evil and spirit release.

Components
In addition to verbal and somatic components, casting this spell required several material components. These included a fresh corpse and a freshly excised patch of skin from the spellcaster's target. The removal of this flesh could cause minor permanent damage to the recipient's overall constitution, harm that could only be reversed with a wish spell or healed with restoration.

Notable Users
 Mezzalcat, a drow necromancer.
 Sammaster, the necromantic founder of the Cult of the Dragon, who inscribed the spell within the Tome of the Dragon.
 Talib al-Ysawis, a Zakharan deathslayer-type necromancer.

## Coinage in Thay

Coinage within the nation of Thay was rarely minted, as by the 15 century DR they used the coinage of other realms as much as possible.

The standard Thayan-minted coins were flat plaques,  tall, in the shape of an inverted simple keystone ("tall" trapezoids with the small end at the top). They bore the symbol of Thaymount on both sides, in opposite vertical orientations, with a hole pierced in their center to allow for stringing multiple coins together on a ring. Each was made of the metal or alloy that they represented – copper, silver, electrum, gold, and platinum.

In the realms outside of Thay, many shunned Thayan coinage out of a common fear that the coins would be magically cursed. In the 14 century DR, Thayan coins were occasionally found in use in the nation of Tethyr, though only by the most experienced and traveled of merchants.

## Coinsharp

Coinsharp was a rare arcane alteration spell from the first level of magic that allowed a wizard to transform a coin into a blade and vice versa.

Effects
With a touch, the spellcaster was able to transform a blade, such as a sword, dagger, scimitar, etc., into a polished golden coin or a golden coin – into a bladed weapon. The blade was always formed to fit perfectly into the caster's hand. The transformed weapon or coin appeared perfectly mundane with a slight radiance of transmutation magic. The appearance of the weapon or coin was determined by the wizard, and the caster with especially high intelligence, wit, and concentration could use coinsharp to transform the item into an exact copy of another weapon if able to closely examine the items they were copying immediately before the casting.

The transformation lasted for a day at the very basic magical proficiency, and the duration increased with the mage's skills. Once the spell expired, the transmuted item returned to its former shape. If the transformed coin or weapon were destroyed or melted or severely damaged in some other way, the spell immediately broke, reverting the transformation.

Components
Coinsharp required verbal, somatic, and material components to be cast. Is material components were a pinch of iron shavings and a fleck of gold or a gold coin shaving.

History
The coinsharp spell was known to Elminster Aumar of Shadowdale and it was among the spells exchanged between the members of The Wizards Three during their visit to Earth and raiding larders of Ed Greenwood of Canada. The spell was brought over to the world of Oerth by Mordenkainen and lady Rautheene, members of the same de facto group.

## Consumption

Consumption, also known as tuberculosis, was a dangerous and potentially deadly non-magical disease that was present on Toril.

Effects
Consumption caused the infected individual to waste away, gradually "consuming" their vitality until they expired. It might also cause symptoms such as sudden weight-loss and vomiting. The disease was regarded as one of the most dangerous mundane diseases, more than even smallpox or spotted fever.

Treatment
Attention from a caregiver or herbalist might slow the progression of consumption. It was said that burdock could be used as a treatment.

History
Gwynneth, leader of the first human settlers of the Moonshae Isles, died of consumption in the .

In the, seven followers of Talona led by Tessurch Quorl Vemmil unleashed a virulent form of consumption in the city of Keczulla, Amn. This plague killed many citizens, and was intended to undermine the authority of Meisarch Thayze Selemchant, the leader of the Council of Six. However, their plans were intercepted, and while the outbreak was allowed to happen by the Meisarch's spies, the perpetrators were revealed to the public. An angry mob then killed them and destroyed their bodies beyond recognition.

In the, there was an outbreak of Dream Fever in Daggerdale, a magical illness that caused consumption in its victims.

Following the events of the Spellplague in the, exposure to the plaguelands of Halruaa could cause a magical variant of the disease known as Halruaan consumption.

As of the late 15 century DR, consumption was the subject of an exaggeratively melancholy song composed in Sarifal known as Oh, Father Dear.

Rumors & Legends
Among death priests who worshiped gods of pestilence—sometimes called "plague priests"—consumption was said to flow from the very breath of their toxic deities.

## Company of the Gryphon

The Company of the Gryphon (also seen as the Company of the Griffon) was an adventuring company active for a few hundred years and later a mercenary company active in the mid–14 century DR. They were credited with discovering the lost dwarven city of Gauntlgrym.
The original write-ups of Namarra cover events "Within the last five hundred years…" but key events were later dated to centuries earlier. As a result, the subsequent events seem spread out more than intended. This is evident with the Company of the Gryphon potentially being active for several centuries, rather than the original one century. Moreover, the story of Namarra calls the Company of the Gryphon "a band of adventurers", while Forgotten Realms Campaign Set declares them "a large... party of mercenaries". Thus, these may represent the same long-running adventuring/mercenary company or different companies operating under the same name in different eras. Nevertheless, the two are included here for completeness and ease of use.

History
Early History
At some point, the Company of the Gryphon killed a goblin wielding an enchanted sword named Ghaur. The company's then leader, the warrior named Flar, claimed the sword and found it was the legendary Namarra, the Sword that Never Sleeps, which the goblins of the Valley of Khedrun had looted in the plundering of Mirabar during the Goblin Wars in .It is unclear when this occurred. The sources say the goblins had the sword "for almost two hundred seasons", but it is unknown if this is meant to be 200 years (e.g., 200 winters) or only 50 years (four seasons per year). Moreover, Namarra's timeline has been stretched by later dating, so it can only be some time between c. 800 DR or c. 950 DR and the 1270s DR. As the timeline is stretched, both presumed dates are difficult to fit—Flar may have the sword for up to ~470 or ~320 years and seems very long-lived.

Later, to pay for training in the combat arts, Flar gave Namarra to Thulmar One-Eye of Port Llast around the 1270s DR.

Gauntlgrym
In the mid-1300s DR, an unidentified person in Waterdeep had discovered the location of the lost dwarven city of Gauntlgrym, reputed to contain much magic and wealth. To explore it on his behalf, he hired the Company of the Gryphon, then a mercenary company numbering thirty members. On their expedition, they found a decaying entrance to the dwarf hold in a high hidden valley. However, only three members returned, having fled the company soon after..

These three made it back to Waterdeep early in the . They triumphantly announced their discovery at the Copper Cup festhall, and the Company of the Gryphon were credited with discovering Gauntlgrym that year. They began spending prodigiously on new weapons and armor for another expedition. Meanwhile, several Waterdeep-based adventurers began investigating, not only the location of the entrance to Gauntlgrym but also the fates of the rest of the Company of the Gryphon and the identity of the one who'd sent them to their dooms. Answers, however, remained unknown as of Ches of that year.

Nevertheless, either a week or a season later, the survivors returned to Gauntlgrym to retrieve its treasures, and did not return, not that year nor the next, nor a decade since.

The Knights of Myth Drannor would later re-discover Gauntlgrym by 1358 DR, and survived.

Known Members
 Flar, a warrior and leader of the early company

Appendix
Background
As reported in correspondence with The Hooded One, the Company of the Gryphon originated in a library-group campaign run by Ed Greenwood in the 1980s while working as a librarian in Toronto. The discovery of Gauntlgrym/Gauntulgrym was an event he ran for the Company of the Gryphon and previously for his home-game group the Knights of Myth Drannor around 1982, hence both groups finding the city in the lore.

## Concussion burst

Concussion burst, also known as concussion blast, was a psionic power of the psychokinesis discipline that allowed a manifester to unleash a harmful blast of telekinetic force at an opponent.

Effects
The manifester of concussion blast could choose a single target, either a creature or an object, anywhere within a range of  to unleash a blast of telekinetic force. This range was further extended in increments of  based upon how skilled the manifester was. Creatures or objects that were fully concealed were invalid targets. And while any object could be targeted by the power, only non-magical objects could be harmed by the blast.

By focusing their psychic energy, a manifester could augment concussion blast to be more adverse, to target one or more additional creatures or objects, or both. In the case of the latter augmentation, any additional target had to be within  of another.

Following the Spellplague and the nature of psionics changing once more, the blast of telekinetic force became more harmful and manifested outward as a wave, effecting all creatures in its path, and caused those affected by it to fall over.

Displays
When used this power manifested an auditory display.

Users
This power was knowable by psions and wilders, as well as ardents and divine minds who followed the force mantle.

Concussion blast was innately known by embracs and psurlons.

It was also commonly found in the psionic repertoire of githzerai.

Known/Notable Users
 Arvin, a human psion.
 The Mind Shard of Pandorym, the imprisoned form of the eponymous elder evil.
 Raulothim, a great wyrm emerald dragon.

Appendix
Background
In 3rd edition psionics, there existed a power simply known as concussion, as well as five other powers that were stated to have the same effect, but did more or less damage than the base concussion or could affect multiple targets. When psionics were updated for v3.5e in the Expanded Psionics Handbook, these six powers were consolidated into this singular power, concussion blast.

## Cocktail

Cocktails were elaborate drinks, prepared on the spot and were made using several ingredients. They were known as brightsongs in Silverymoon, Neverwinter, and Waterdeep; manyslakes in Waterdeep, Scornubel, Iriaebor, Cormyr, and Sembia; ralivarthrem in Amn and Tethyr; ravalankh in Calimshan and the Tashalar; and drarraval in Turmish, the Vilhon Reach, and Chessenta. They were served in large establishments, such as the Yawning Portal, and found on other planes, such as the Wandering Emporium and Dragon's Pride in Avernus.

Description
Manyslakes of Faerûn were widely varied across the realms, from simple concoctions of several types of alcoholic drinks, non-alcoholic drinks, spices, to complex and showy colorful drinks that produced steam, flames, or were enchanted via magic.

Notable Manyslakes
Blazing Bloody Jack, a sweet and spicy drink from Avernus that posessed the effects of a potion of heroism.
Delayed Blast a strong drink of sarrak, a juice made from cherries called red tenth, and the garden vegetable sweetstalk.
Dragon's Bite, a drink of green mint wine, pepper brandy, cinnamon powder, and licorice root.
Dragon's Morning Breath, a drink that tastes like "Dragon's Morning Piss."
Fizzy Cherry Delight, a sweet fizzy drink.
Flaming Gullet, a drink made with klaraunth (a strong and clear distilled barley alcohol), a distillate of hot red radishes, a distillate of horseradish, and finely crushed and powdered chestnuts.
Joker's Sky, a blue drink from Avernus, topped with whipped foam that posessed the effects of a potion of flying.
Red Rum Swirl, a sweet drink of cherry brandy, rum, almond brandy and stirred-in caramel.
Salubra Slinger, a fizzy berry-flavored drink from Avernus that posessed the effects of an elixir of health.
The Moon's Head Brace, an immensely alcoholic drink white drink flavored with mushrooms.
The Walking Furniture, an immensely alcoholic drink made with hard apple cider mixed with a taint of brownish liquor.
Tyr's Juice of Justice, an orange drink that temporarily boosted the drinker's musculature through illusion magic.
Volo's Folly, a drink that made the imbiber's skin sparkle.
Yeti's Breath, a freezing cold drink of crushed ice and tapdragon with added darsargar and menthol.

Other notable cocktails were: Tansar's Dance, Marthoun's Flagon, Dragondown, Ladydagger, Bright Blade, Wyvernblood, Sea Ward Slake, Snowfire, Nightfire, Lightning Bolt, Battle Banner, Merchants' Tears, Harbour Foam, Stag at Bay, and Caravan Lantern.

History
In the late 15 century DR, West Caraway Acres, a mansion outside Neverwinter that belonged to the eccentric dragonborn wizard Torlinn Shrake, shared a variety of magic-enhanced cocktails during his lavish parties.

## Communication mantle

The Communication mantle was a psionic mantle that granted ardents and divine minds an array of psionics powers and abilities derived from the universal concept and philosophy of communication.

Deities

Abilities
Those who followed the communication mantle became far more eloquent and skilled communicators when psionically focused, making them more better equipped to resolve matters diplomatically.

The psychic aura exuded by divine minds of the communication mantle created an effect similar to mindlink between the manifester and their nearby allies, so long as they remained within the aura's radius.

Powers
Novice manifesters were able to send telepathic messages with missive and subtly alter the behaviors of others with attraction, psionic charm, and telempathic projection. Manifesters of some experience gained greater telepathic abilities with mass missive and psionic tongues, as well as greater manipulation with psionic suggestion. As a manifester progressed further they learned how to cooperatively use their psionics with metaconcert and telepathically talk from great distances with correspond. Masters of this mantle obtained the power of metafaculty, allowing them to discern information on any subject.

## Corruption and Madness mantle

The Corruption and Madness mantle was a psionic mantle that granted ardents and divine minds an array of psionics powers and abilities derived from the universal concept and philosophy of insanity.

Deities

Abilities
Those who followed the Corruption and Madness mantle gained terrible insights into its associated concept, making them impervious to being confused or driven mad while psionically focused.

The psychic aura exuded by divine minds of the Corruption and Madness mantle wrought disturbance in the minds of all who opposed them, making it more difficult for enemies within the radius of the aura to cast spells or manifest psionic powers, as well as increased the difficulty of using spell-like and psionic-like abilities.

Powers
Novice manifesters were able to modestly disquiet the minds of their foes with brain lock, primal fear, and psionic daze. Manifesters of some experience learned how to further hinder a creature's capacity to function with mental turmoil and mindwipe. As a manifester progressed further they obtained decerebrate and insanity, allowing them to cause permanent damage to a creature's mind. Masters of this mantle obtained the power to significantly warp the consciousnesses of others with microcosm, allowing them to trap creatures within their own mindscape.

## Conflict mantle

The Conflict mantle was a psionic mantle that granted ardents and divine minds an array of psionics powers and abilities derived from the universal concept or philosophy of conflict.

Deities

Abilities
Those who followed the conflict mantle became more in tune with martial concepts, becoming proficient in the use of a weapon type they previously weren't.In mechanical terms, the Conflict mantle granted "...the Weapon Focus feat as a bonus feat with a weapon of your choice."

The psychic aura exuded by divine minds of the conflict mantle made the manifester and their nearby allies more proficient at landing devastating strikes in combat.

Novice manifesters gained the power to infuse weapons with psionic energy with metaphysical weapon and gain brief glimpses of the future of a conflict with offensive prescience. As a manifester progressed further they obtained the power to brutally strike the enemy's mind with psychic crush and to mold weapons to their flesh with graft weapon. Masters of this mantle obtained the power spirit of war, allowing them to exude a martial aura that improved their battle prowess.

## Consumption mantle

The Consumption mantle was a psionic mantle that granted ardents and divine minds an array of psionics powers and abilities derived from the universal concept or philosophy of consumption, themed around parasitically drawing power from other creatures.

Deities

Abilities
Those who followed the consumption mantle gained the unique psionic power to expend a psionic focus to moderately heal their own wounds when within  of a wounded creature.

The psychic aura exuded by divine minds of the consumption mantle allowed the manifester to expend a psionic focus whenever a power was manifested within the radius of their aura. When done, this leeched psionic energy away from the manifestation and added it to the divine mind's mental reserve.

Powers
Novice manifesters gained a deleterious, self-healing touch with hungry touch and the power to temporarily exhibit the unique psionic abilities of others with feat leech. Masters of this mantle obtained the power apopsi, allowing them to outright remove the powers ingrained within a psionics user's mind.

After surviving the trials and tribulations of the adventuring life into old age, the group settled down in a retirement home to while away their remaining days. ## Cornelius Latrimor

Cornelius Latrimor was one of the Magistrates of Cormyr, who performed work in the town of Wheloon in the late 15 century DR.

Activities
Cornelius worked at the Wheloon Docks alongside Magistrates Abella Toth, Barthold Moncrief, and Celia Pendrick as they oversaw the operations of the prison and investigated criminals.

History
During the Shadovar invasion of Wheloon, Cornelius was charged with the interrogation of Sharran cultist Dedryk Black after he was captured by adventurers from the world of Eberron and taken back to Wheloon. Having been unsuccessful in learning anything, he let the adventurers who had caught him twice take a turn. Though he spoke mostly threats and curses, Dedryk did mention that he had passed through the shadows themselves to freedom, and was willing to entertain a small measure of cooperation to ensure the safety of himself and his followers. Before the interrogation could proceed much further, however, the whole area was assaulted by the forces of Returned Netheril as they overlapped the docks with the Shadowfell itself, allowing a small army of living shadows and enraged prisoners to burst into the Cormyrean position from the inside. While the defenders fought off the attack, the shadar-kai assassin Teralyn shadowstepped into the Magistrates office, slew Cornelius, and sent Dedryk back into the shadows to freedom. Before Teralyn could escape herself, she was cornered by the vengeful heroes from Eberron and slain in battle.

## Court of the Three

The Court of the Three was the self-proclaimed successor to Returned Netheril founded following the death of Lord Telamont Tanthul and the destruction of Thultanthar. It was named for its leaders—Lelavdra Tanthul, Manarlume Tanthul, and Gwelt—who referred to themselves collectively as the Three.

Activities
The Three were ambitious and specialized in subterfuge. In the short-term, they aimed to create a refuge for their fellow Thultanthan survivors. Their stated goal was to bring together Shadovar and to preserve Thultanthan culture in the face of the many foes that Returned Netheril had amassed. To this end, they advocated for a much more subtle presence than their predecessors, keeping to themselves and focusing on avoiding and identifying enemies while finding new allies. They sought out fellow Thultanthans and tried to integrate them into their faction, sometimes with manipulation or seduction.

While the Three claimed specifically to be the rightful heirs to Thultanthar, their future ambitions extended to the surviving cities of Returned Netheril and (perhaps) to conquest.

Base of Operations
The Court of the Three operated out of the Citadel of the Raven, specifically from one of the most well-maintained of its ruined fortresses. There they received new recruits and amassed supplies. They kept their activities magically concealed.

Relationships
The Court of the Three had many enemies, and largely regarded all of Toril as hostile or potentially hostile to them.

They kept a close eye on the activities of the Zhentarim, especially once they too began efforts to reclaim parts of the Citadel of the Raven. Hidden by their magics, the Three used deception, manipulation, and assassination to keep the unknowing Zhents in check.

History
Following the fall of Thultanthar in the, Lord Telamont Tanthul was dead and his princes were dead or missing. In this power vacuum, the Three came together and declared themselves the rightful heirs to that city: sisters Lelavdra and Manarlume were both granddaughters of Lord Telamont, and thus claimed rulership as their birthright, while the arcanist Gwelt had been a trusted lieutenant of Lord Tanthul, who had granted him extraordinary powers of command. Declaring themselves to be fast friends and allies—if not lovers—the Three agreed that the Princes of Shade had been foolish and prideful, and so designed their Court of the Three to avoid falling into the same trap.

From their base at the Citadel of the Raven, Gwelt ranged out to find and convince fellow Shadovar to join the Three's cause while the sisters used their wiles to cement the loyalty of the most critical new recruits. While their recruiting efforts were more successful than they had anticipated, a large number of arcanists rejected them, preferring not to follow a new master but to pursue their own ambitions.

As the stresses of leadership mounted, it was unclear whether the avowed friendship between the Three would last.

Members
By late 1487 DR, the Three had managed to rally about sixty Shadovar arcanists to their cause, largely of lower ranks. Additionally, they had been joined by twenty non-Shadovar former Thultanthans.

## Corwell's Steeple

Corwell's Steeple was a tower on Crane Point in the Highlands of the island of Gwynneth in the Moonshae Isles. As of the mid-to-late 15 century DR, it was all that remained of what had once been a citadel and temple dedicated to the moon.

Description
In its ruined state, the Steeple was a tall stone spire adorned with broken arches. Halfway up the tower was a gaping hole where monsters could perch, and at the very top was a platform once dedicated to observing the moon, but since had also become a perch for flying beasts.

Geography
The Steeple was located at the tip of the Crane Point promontory on the edge of Ulls lake.

History
The temple had been built by the humans of Corwell. After the takeover of Gwynneth by the fey of Sarifal, the temple and its surrounding defenses fell into ruin. The Steeple came to be home to rainbow cranes, hippogriffs, and the rare mated pair of wild griffons. The fey enjoyed watching these creatures from afar as they indulged in hunting, drinking, and music on Crane Point.

Inhabitants of Sarifal wishing to smuggle themselves in or out of the isolated realm could arrange for a domesticated hippogriff to meet them inconspicuously at the Steeple. This was the plan hatched by Valeanne, Tiana, and Shamasar in the late 1460s DR when they schemed to steal Princess Amaranth away from Karador to save her from her half-sister, High Lady Ordalf. The plot was to arrange for a hippogriff rider to take her to the court of Queen Erliza Daressin on Snowdown, but they were betrayed and intercepted by drow mercenaries sent by Ordalf's son, Prince Araithe, who were intent on recapturing the nine-year-old princess. The drow attacked both the party as they sped toward the Steeple as well as the riders waiting at the Steeple, although this angered the monsters who nested there. While Amaranth was successfully handed off to a hippogriff rider during the heat of battle, this rider was badly injured and never arrived at Snowdown. It would be a decade before she was finally found.
